  • Moroccan Home Decor Trend - rich patterns drawing eyes from walls

What the Experts Say About Hiding Wall Flaws Creatively

Creative wall styling has been recognised by professional designers as one of the most practical and accessible ways to deal with wall imperfections — without touching the wall itself.

The approach goes well beyond simple covering up. When done thoughtfully, it transforms a liability into a genuine design feature — and that's a principle that professional interior designers have advocated for years. As outlined in the resource 12 Ways to Hide a Flaw on the Wall, strategic decor placement — including art, mirrors, shelves, and textiles — is a legitimate and widely recommended design solution, not just a workaround. The emphasis across all professional guidance is on making the fix look entirely intentional.

The most important shift in mindset is moving from "how do I hide this?" to "how do I make this wall beautiful?" Those are surprisingly different questions — and the second one leads to far more creative results. When you approach the problem area as a design opportunity rather than a flaw, the solutions you reach for are bolder, more interesting, and ultimately more effective.

That's the approach I take with every client, and it's the approach I'd encourage you to take in your own home — rented or owned, large or small.

WATCH: The Ultimate Guide to a Stunning Gallery Wall

Ready to Transform Your Problem Wall?

Wall imperfections are genuinely not the disaster they feel like in the moment. With the right art, the right arrangement, and a bit of intention, even the most battle-scarred wall can become the feature you're most proud of in your home.

Whether you're renting and can't touch the walls, or you just don't want the hassle and expense of plastering and repainting, bohemian wall art gives you a creative, affordable, and deeply personal alternative. A tapestry, a gallery wall, a large canvas, a macramé piece — any of these can do a job that a pot of filler never quite manages: they make the room feel loved.

how do color schemes work in open concep.bodyHtml:
Colour schemes in open concept homes work best when you treat the entire space as one connected canvas — choosing a unifying base colour, then using accent colours, wall art, textiles, and lighting to define each zone without chopping the space up with hard boundaries. The goal is flow, not uniformity.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in the middle of your open plan living space, paint chart in hand, and thought — if I paint the kitchen a different colour to the lounge, will it look like two separate flats? Or worse, if I keep it all the same, will the whole thing look like one giant magnolia box? I've been there, and so have almost every client I've worked with. The good news is that wall art and the right colour strategy can completely transform how an open plan space feels — without a single drop of paint if you'd rather not commit.

Quick answer: Colour schemes in open concept homes rely on a shared base colour across all zones, with accent colours, art, textiles, and decor used to give each area its own personality. Layering these elements — not just relying on paint — is what creates both cohesion and visual interest.

Open concept living has been a fixture of modern home design for years now, and it genuinely offers a beautiful sense of space and light. But it also throws up a real decorating puzzle: how do you make a kitchen, a dining area, and a lounge all feel purposeful and distinct when there are no walls between them? The answer lies in understanding colour — not just on your walls, but across your unique wall art, your furniture choices, your rugs, and your unique home decor throughout the space. Get that right, and you've got a home that feels both cohesive and alive.

How to Transition Paint Colours Between Open Concept Zones

Transitioning paint colours in an open plan space is less about where you stop one colour and start another, and more about finding a logical, architectural reason for the change. A structural column, a change in ceiling height, the edge of a kitchen island, or even the shift from a tiled floor to wooden boards — all of these give you a natural "excuse" to introduce a new colour.

The mistake I always see is people trying to transition colours mid-wall with no anchor point. It looks arbitrary and can feel unsettling, even if you can't immediately put your finger on why. Always let an architectural feature do the heavy lifting for you.

Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. An open plan kitchen and living area in a modern British home, showing a natural colour transition between zones — warm greige walls in the living zone, soft sage-tinted cabinetry in the kitchen zone, divided by a structural pillar or kitchen island edge. Wooden flooring flows throughout, connecting both areas. A South Asian woman stands near the island, casually looking across the living space, holding a mug — relaxed, candid pose, morning light streaming in from a side window.]]

Practical ways to transition colour between zones

  • Use an architectural feature (column, beam, archway) as your natural colour break point.
  • Try a tone-on-tone approach — a slightly deeper or lighter version of the same hue in each zone.
  • Use the same paint colour throughout and let flooring materials signal the zone change instead.
  • Paint an accent wall within a specific zone to define it without clashing with adjacent areas.
  • Use open shelving as a visual divider — the items styled on it carry the colour story forward.
  • Consider a darker ceiling in the dining zone for intimacy while keeping walls continuous.
Pro Tip: When in doubt, use the 60-30-10 rule per zone — 60% base colour, 30% secondary, 10% accent — and make sure the 60% base is the same across every zone for instant cohesion.

Choosing a Versatile Base Colour for Open Floor Plans

Your base colour is the one that ties the whole space together, so it needs to work across very different functional areas — a relaxed sofa zone, a bright kitchen, a dining table that sees everything from Sunday breakfast to candlelit suppers. That is a lot to ask of one colour, which is why versatility is the single most important quality here.

In my experience, warm neutrals — think soft whites with a hint of warm beige, greige, or the palest warm grey — consistently outperform cool whites and stark greys in open plan homes. Cool colours can look great in a bathroom or bedroom but feel clinical once they sprawl across 40 square metres.

Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A spacious open plan British home interior, all walls painted in a warm greige/pale off-white tone. The space includes a linen sofa in the foreground, a round dining table in the middle ground, and light oak kitchen cabinetry in the background — showing how one base colour can unify all three zones elegantly. A Black British woman in her 30s stands near the dining table arranging fresh flowers, candid and natural, afternoon light.]]

Top base colour choices for open floor plans

  • Warm white: Classic, flexible, brightens the space — avoid stark cool whites which can feel cold at scale.
  • Greige (grey-beige): Endlessly versatile, works with wood tones, dark accents, and pastels alike.
  • Pale sage green: Brings freshness and warmth without reading as a bold colour choice.
  • Soft clay or terracotta-adjacent: Adds depth and warmth, especially in north-facing open plan spaces.
  • Off-white with a pink undertone: Surprisingly warm and flattering in evening lighting.

I once helped a client in a ground-floor flat who had gone for a very cool grey throughout her open plan. During the day it was fine, but in the evenings it turned a strange lavender-blue under her warm LED lighting. We repainted with a warm greige and the transformation was instant — the space felt cosy and connected rather than cold and institutional.

Pro Tip: Always test your base colour at A3 size or larger on the actual wall. A small paint chip tells you almost nothing — the same colour reads completely differently at scale and in your specific light.

Using Accent Colours to Define Personality and Zones

Once your base colour is locked in, accent colours become your secret weapon. They are what stops a beautifully cohesive space from looking beige and forgettable. In an open concept layout, accent colours do double duty — they add visual interest AND signal to the eye that you are now in a different zone.

The key is choosing accent colours that share an underlying undertone with your base. Warm base? Choose warm accents — terracotta, deep mustard, rust, olive. Cool base? Dusty blues, soft lavenders, and muted greens will feel natural. Mix warm and cool accent colours in the same space and things quickly start to feel restless.

RIGHT SIDE labelled "Strategic Accent Colours — Clear Zones" showing the same room with a consistent base and deliberate accent groupings: one warm rust cluster in the living zone, one deep teal in the dining zone, clearly delineating the areas.]]

How to use accent colours strategically in open concept zones

  • Assign one or two accent colours per zone — don't scatter them randomly across the whole floor plan.
  • Use cushions, throws, a rug, and one piece of wall art in the same accent to "anchor" each zone visually.
  • Repeat a single accent colour — even just one item — in each zone to create a connecting thread.
  • Keep your kitchen accent colours in hardware and accessories rather than on walls (grease and steam affect painted surfaces).
  • A bold accent on a single dining room wall creates intimacy without breaking the open plan flow.
[[PRODUCT|botanical wall art prints with warm earthy accent tones]]
Real Example: I worked with a family who had a large L-shaped open plan. We used their children's artwork (properly framed, it looked brilliant) as the accent colour palette inspiration — all warm yellows and corals — and then repeated those tones in cushions in the lounge and a table runner in the dining zone. The whole space felt like it belonged to them, not a show home.

How Lighting Conditions Affect Colour Choices in Open Layouts

Lighting is the single most underestimated factor in open plan colour choices, and it is the one that bites people hardest. An open concept space often has wildly different light conditions within the same floor plate — south-facing kitchen bathed in sun all afternoon, north-facing living end that never sees direct light. The same paint colour will look completely different in each.

This is not just about natural light. The type of artificial lighting you use — warm vs. cool LEDs, pendant height, number of points — changes how every colour reads at night. I've seen warm terracotta turn muddy and dark under cool overhead LEDs, and soft sage green look almost neon under the wrong bulb temperature.

[[IMG|lighting-colour-open-plan-zones|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. An open plan living and dining space photographed at dusk, showing the contrast between the naturally-lit kitchen end and the warm pendant-lit dining zone — demonstrating how the same warm greige wall reads slightly differently in natural vs. artificial light. Wall sconces add warmth beside a large mirror. A mixed-race British couple in their 40s, a man and a woman, sit at the dining table in conversation, candles lit, warm and relaxed.]]

Lighting factors to check before committing to a colour

  • Test your chosen colour at different times of day — morning, midday, and evening with your actual artificial lights on.
  • North-facing ends of an open plan benefit from warm-toned colours; avoid cool greys that can look stark.
  • South-facing areas can handle cooler tones because natural light warms them up organically.
  • Use warm-white LED bulbs (2700K–3000K) throughout open plan spaces for consistent colour rendering.
  • Pendant lights over a dining zone or island define the area and add a different quality of light intentionally.
  • Mirrors used as wall decor bounce light into darker zones and make colours look more consistent.
Pro Tip: If your open plan space has dramatically different light at each end, choose your base colour by testing it in the darkest corner. A colour that works there will look even better in the brighter zones — but not the other way around.
[[PRODUCT|large decorative mirror for open plan living room]]

Achieving Colour Harmony Across Connected Living Spaces

Colour harmony in an open concept home does not mean every surface is the same colour — it means every colour in the space feels like it belongs to the same family. Think of it like a wardrobe: every item does not need to be identical, but they should all work together when laid out side by side.

The most reliable method I use with clients is the "colour story thread" — picking three to four colours that appear throughout the entire open plan, just in different proportions in different zones. One of those colours anchors every zone; the others rotate in supporting and accent roles.

[[IMG|colour-harmony-open-concept-living|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A wide-angle shot of a harmonious open plan living, dining and kitchen space in a British home — warm greige walls, olive green cushions in the lounge, a terracotta table runner in the dining zone, and warm brass kitchen hardware — showing how three accent colours echo across zones without clashing. A Black British man in his 30s stands near a bookshelf styling objects, natural and candid.]]

Colour harmony methods that work in open layouts

Harmony Method How It Works Best For
Monochromatic One colour family in light, mid, and deep tones across zones Minimalist or Japandi styles
Analogous Neighbouring colours on the wheel — e.g. sage, olive, teal Natural, botanical, or boho styles
Complementary (muted) Opposite colours but desaturated — e.g. dusty terracotta + muted teal Eclectic or maximalist spaces
Neutral + one bold accent All base neutrals with one consistent bold colour used sparingly throughout Contemporary or Scandi spaces

Pro Tip: Pull a colour palette from one piece of art or a textile you already love in the space. Nature has already done the colour harmony work for you in most good-quality prints and woven textiles — trust the source material.

How Wall Art and Decor Can Reinforce or Replace Paint Colour Zoning

Here is the thing not enough people talk about: you do not always need paint to create zones in an open concept home. Wall art, mirrors, shelving arrangements, and wall-hung decor can do almost all of the same visual work — and they are far easier to change your mind about.

A large-scale art print on one wall of a lounge zone immediately signals "this is the living area" without a single drop of paint. A gallery wall of botanical prints above a dining table tells your eye "sit down, you are in the dining zone." Decor anchors zones just as effectively as colour, and it carries personality that plain paint simply cannot.

[[IMG|wall-art-decor-zone-definition|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. An open plan kitchen and lounge where the living zone is anchored by a large macramé wall hanging above a linen sofa, and the dining zone is defined by a cluster of hanging woven pendants and a potted trailing plant on a wall shelf. Warm neutral walls throughout. A young East Asian woman sits on the sofa reading, relaxed, afternoon light, candid.]]

Ways wall art and decor create zones without paint

  • A large-format art piece (canvas, framed print, or textile artwork) anchors a seating zone instantly.
  • A gallery wall arranged above a dining table signals the dining area clearly and beautifully.
  • Open wall shelving styled with colour-coordinated objects defines the zone and adds depth.
  • A macramé or textile wall hanging brings warmth and texture to a lounge zone without any commitment.
  • Mirrors used in the darker end of the open plan both brighten the space and mark it out visually.
  • A wall-mounted light fixture or sconce above a specific zone acts as a spatial signal as well as a light source.
[[PRODUCT|large format abstract canvas wall art for open plan living zones]]

I once styled an open plan flat for a renter who couldn't touch the walls. The landlord had painted everything the same pale cream. We used a huge woven wall textile in warm terracotta and cream above the sofa, a set of framed botanical prints above the dining table, and a round mirror in the kitchen zone. Visitors genuinely asked what colour the kitchen had been painted — they didn't realise it was all the same wall colour throughout. That is the power of well-placed decor.

Real Example: Renters and those not ready to commit to paint — this approach is made for you. Invest in three strong pieces of wall art or decor for each zone, and let them carry the colour story instead of the walls.

Colour Schemes for Open Concept Homes with Specific Style Aesthetics

Your style aesthetic shapes everything about your colour choices — not just which colours you pick, but how you layer them, how bold you go, and which materials you bring in alongside them. Colour schemes for open concept homes look very different depending on whether you are going boho, Scandi, or full maximalist.

It helps to have a clear style anchor before you start choosing colours — otherwise you end up with a space that is a bit of everything and a lot of nothing. Here is how I approach the three most popular styles I am asked about.

Style-specific colour guidance for open plan homes

  • Boho: Warm terracotta, rust, dusty pink, off-white, and ochre. Layer lots of textures — jute, linen, macramé. Zone with textile art and plants rather than paint.
  • Scandi: White or very pale greige base, one or two muted accent colours (dusty blue, sage, blush), natural wood tones throughout. Simplicity is the zone-definer.
  • Japandi: Warm white or pale clay, deep charcoal or black accents used sparingly, natural materials — linen, rattan, wood. Negative space does the zoning work.
  • Maximalist: Rich, deep jewel tones — emerald, sapphire, plum, ochre. Each zone can have its own bold colour IF they share an underlying warm or cool tone direction.
  • Contemporary/Modern: Greige or warm white base, bold accent in a single colour used consistently. Clean lines and minimal clutter let the colour scheme breathe.
  • Eclectic: Anything goes — but choose one colour that threads through every zone as a connecting stitch to keep it from feeling chaotic.

Pro Tip: If you love maximalist colour but share the space with someone who prefers calm, compromise by going maximalist in one zone (perhaps the dining area) and Scandi-neutral in the others. The contrast between zones can actually be a feature rather than a conflict.

The Role of Furniture and Textiles in Tying Colour Schemes Together

Furniture and textiles are arguably the most powerful colour carriers in an open plan space — more powerful than paint, actually, because they exist in three dimensions, they absorb and reflect light differently, and they can be changed without a decorator's invoice. A sofa, a rug, a set of dining chairs, a throw — these are your real colour tools.

The classic mistake is choosing furniture in a vacuum — picking a sofa in the shop, a dining table online, kitchen stools from somewhere else — without running them against each other first. In an open plan space where everything is visible simultaneously, this almost always results in a colour mismatch that no amount of paint can fix.

The palette is warm and cohesive. A South Asian man in his late 30s arranges cushions on the sofa, casual and candid, natural daylight.]]

Textile and furniture colour tips for open plan spaces

  • Choose your largest furniture pieces (sofa, dining table, rug) first — they set the colour temperature of the whole space.
  • A large area rug is one of the most effective zone-definers you can buy — and it brings enormous colour into a space that paint cannot touch.
  • Cushions and throws are your cheapest colour experiment — swap them seasonally to refresh the palette.
  • Dining chairs are often underestimated as colour vehicles — a set of chairs in a bold or contrasting tone can define the dining zone beautifully.
  • Curtains or blinds carry a surprising amount of colour — make sure they are in the conversation from the start.
  • Repeat one textile colour (even in a small quantity) in each zone — a cushion here, a vase there — to create a colour thread that reads naturally from every angle.

Pro Tip: Before buying any large piece of furniture, place a large sheet of paper in the colour you are considering on the floor or against the sofa. Step back and live with it for a day. It sounds daft but it has saved many of my clients from an expensive mistake.

I'll use a common configuration: lounge zone, dining zone, and kitchen zone all sharing one floor plate, with a large window on one end and the kitchen at the other.

Zone-by-zone colour anchoring tips

  • Lounge zone: Your largest rug grounds the colour palette here. Choose it first. Wall decor above the sofa — a textile hanging, a set of art prints, or a gallery wall — defines the zone's personality.
  • Dining zone: The dining table and chairs carry the most colour. A pendant light above the table does double duty — it zones the area and adds a warm colour note. A shelf or sideboard with styled objects brings in the accent colours.
  • Kitchen zone: Cabinet colour is your biggest colour decision here. If walls are neutral, cabinets can go bolder — sage, navy, or deep grey. Repeat one colour from the lounge in ceramic accessories or small appliances.
  • Transition points: Identify where one zone ends and another begins. Put something there — a plant, a floor lamp, an open shelving unit — to act as a visual "comma" in the space.
  • The connecting thread: Choose one colour that appears somewhere in every zone, even in a small way. This creates subconscious cohesion that reads as "this home is put together" even to guests who couldn't tell you why.

I worked on a long, narrow Victorian terrace conversion where the open plan stretched about twelve metres from front to back. The challenge was keeping it from feeling like a corridor. We anchored each zone with a different rug — same colour family, different scale of pattern — and used a single brass tone in hardware, light fittings, and a few accessories across all three zones. That brass thread made the whole space sing. Nobody asked why it felt cohesive; they just sat down and relaxed. That is exactly what you want.

Real Example: The "connector colour" trick — picking one metallic, one neutral tone, or one shade of green that appears in every single zone, even if just in a small ceramic or a trailing plant — is the single easiest way to make an open plan space feel intentionally designed rather than randomly assembled.

Budget-Friendly Ways to Test and Commit to an Open Concept Colour Palette

Committing to a colour palette across an entire open plan space is genuinely daunting — not just emotionally but financially. Getting it wrong in a big space means a lot of wasted paint, or worse, furniture you need to sell on. The good news is there are very practical ways to test before you commit, and most of them cost very little.

I always tell clients: think of the first round as "renting the colour." You are not marrying it yet. You are just seeing how you get on.

Low-cost ways to test an open plan colour palette

  • Order paint tester pots and apply them to A2 or A3 card, not directly on the wall — you can move them around and test them across all zones.
  • Use cushion covers and throws in your intended accent colours before committing to a sofa or curtains — cushions are your cheapest experiment.
  • Buy one affordable print in your intended accent colour palette and live with it for two weeks before buying more wall art or repainting.
  • Try peel-and-stick paint samples if your wall is already white — some brands offer these and they remove cleanly.
  • Use large pieces of coloured card or even wrapping paper to mock up what a coloured accent wall will look like before painting it.
  • Rearrange and style the furniture you already have in zone formations before spending anything — this often reveals what is actually missing.
  • Visit a local paint store that offers physical colour consultations — many offer this free of charge and it is worth every minute.

Pro Tip: The most budget-friendly route into a new colour palette is always through textiles and art first, paint second. Swap your cushions and throws, buy one or two art prints, and live with the new palette for a month before touching the walls. You will be absolutely certain by then — or happily grateful you did not reach for the paintbrush.

More About Getting Colour Right in Open Plan Homes

Getting colour right in an open concept home is one of the most rewarding decorating challenges you will take on — and the learning curve is genuinely worth it.

The key things to hold onto are: start with a versatile base, use accent colours purposefully to zone and add personality, and remember that paint is only one part of the picture. Wall art, textiles, rugs, lighting, and carefully chosen decor objects all carry colour just as powerfully. For a thorough practical guide on how to actually approach the painting process in an open concept layout — including advice on where to stop and start each colour — I'd recommend reading this guide by How to Paint an Open-Concept Home | Sherwin-Williams, which covers the technical side really well.

The most important thing? Do not let the scale of an open plan space paralyse you into beige inaction. Start small, test often, and build your confidence one zone at a time.

Ready to Start Your Open Concept Colour Story?

I hope this has given you a real, practical framework to approach colour schemes in your open concept home — not just a list of pretty colours, but an actual method for making the space feel considered and cohesive from every angle.

Whether you are starting from scratch, repainting, or simply looking to refresh the feel of your open plan through art and decor rather than a full renovation, the principles here apply. Take it one zone at a time, trust your base colour, and let the textiles and art do far more of the heavy lifting than most people realise.

Colour schemes in open concept homes work best when you treat the entire space as one connected canvas — choosing a unifying base colour, then using accent colours, wall art, textiles, and lighting to define each zone without chopping the space up with hard boundaries. The goal is flow, not uniformity.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in the middle of your open plan living space, paint chart in hand, and thought — if I paint the kitchen a different colour to the lounge, will it look like two separate flats? Or worse, if I keep it all the same, will the whole thing look like one giant magnolia box? I've been there, and so have almost every client I've worked with. The good news is that wall art and the right colour strategy can completely transform how an open plan space feels — without a single drop of paint if you'd rather not commit.

Quick answer: Colour schemes in open concept homes rely on a shared base colour across all zones, with accent colours, art, textiles, and decor used to give each area its own personality. Layering these elements — not just relying on paint — is what creates both cohesion and visual interest.

Open concept living has been a fixture of modern home design for years now, and it genuinely offers a beautiful sense of space and light. But it also throws up a real decorating puzzle: how do you make a kitchen, a dining area, and a lounge all feel purposeful and distinct when there are no walls between them? The answer lies in understanding colour — not just on your walls, but across your unique wall art, your furniture choices, your rugs, and your unique home decor throughout the space. Get that right, and you've got a home that feels both cohesive and alive.

How to Transition Paint Colours Between Open Concept Zones

Transitioning paint colours in an open plan space is less about where you stop one colour and start another, and more about finding a logical, architectural reason for the change. A structural column, a change in ceiling height, the edge of a kitchen island, or even the shift from a tiled floor to wooden boards — all of these give you a natural "excuse" to introduce a new colour.

The mistake I always see is people trying to transition colours mid-wall with no anchor point. It looks arbitrary and can feel unsettling, even if you can't immediately put your finger on why. Always let an architectural feature do the heavy lifting for you.

Practical ways to transition colour between zones

  • Use an architectural feature (column, beam, archway) as your natural colour break point.
  • Try a tone-on-tone approach — a slightly deeper or lighter version of the same hue in each zone.
  • Use the same paint colour throughout and let flooring materials signal the zone change instead.
  • Paint an accent wall within a specific zone to define it without clashing with adjacent areas.
  • Use open shelving as a visual divider — the items styled on it carry the colour story forward.
  • Consider a darker ceiling in the dining zone for intimacy while keeping walls continuous.
Pro Tip: When in doubt, use the 60-30-10 rule per zone — 60% base colour, 30% secondary, 10% accent — and make sure the 60% base is the same across every zone for instant cohesion.

Choosing a Versatile Base Colour for Open Floor Plans

Your base colour is the one that ties the whole space together, so it needs to work across very different functional areas — a relaxed sofa zone, a bright kitchen, a dining table that sees everything from Sunday breakfast to candlelit suppers. That is a lot to ask of one colour, which is why versatility is the single most important quality here.

In my experience, warm neutrals — think soft whites with a hint of warm beige, greige, or the palest warm grey — consistently outperform cool whites and stark greys in open plan homes. Cool colours can look great in a bathroom or bedroom but feel clinical once they sprawl across 40 square metres.

Top base colour choices for open floor plans

  • Warm white: Classic, flexible, brightens the space — avoid stark cool whites which can feel cold at scale.
  • Greige (grey-beige): Endlessly versatile, works with wood tones, dark accents, and pastels alike.
  • Pale sage green: Brings freshness and warmth without reading as a bold colour choice.
  • Soft clay or terracotta-adjacent: Adds depth and warmth, especially in north-facing open plan spaces.
  • Off-white with a pink undertone: Surprisingly warm and flattering in evening lighting.

I once helped a client in a ground-floor flat who had gone for a very cool grey throughout her open plan. During the day it was fine, but in the evenings it turned a strange lavender-blue under her warm LED lighting. We repainted with a warm greige and the transformation was instant — the space felt cosy and connected rather than cold and institutional.

Pro Tip: Always test your base colour at A3 size or larger on the actual wall. A small paint chip tells you almost nothing — the same colour reads completely differently at scale and in your specific light.

Using Accent Colours to Define Personality and Zones

Once your base colour is locked in, accent colours become your secret weapon. They are what stops a beautifully cohesive space from looking beige and forgettable. In an open concept layout, accent colours do double duty — they add visual interest AND signal to the eye that you are now in a different zone.

The key is choosing accent colours that share an underlying undertone with your base. Warm base? Choose warm accents — terracotta, deep mustard, rust, olive. Cool base? Dusty blues, soft lavenders, and muted greens will feel natural. Mix warm and cool accent colours in the same space and things quickly start to feel restless.

How to use accent colours strategically in open concept zones

  • Assign one or two accent colours per zone — don't scatter them randomly across the whole floor plan.
  • Use cushions, throws, a rug, and one piece of wall art in the same accent to "anchor" each zone visually.
  • Repeat a single accent colour — even just one item — in each zone to create a connecting thread.
  • Keep your kitchen accent colours in hardware and accessories rather than on walls (grease and steam affect painted surfaces).
  • A bold accent on a single dining room wall creates intimacy without breaking the open plan flow.

Real Example: I worked with a family who had a large L-shaped open plan. We used their children's artwork (properly framed, it looked brilliant) as the accent colour palette inspiration — all warm yellows and corals — and then repeated those tones in cushions in the lounge and a table runner in the dining zone. The whole space felt like it belonged to them, not a show home.

How Lighting Conditions Affect Colour Choices in Open Layouts

Lighting is the single most underestimated factor in open plan colour choices, and it is the one that bites people hardest. An open concept space often has wildly different light conditions within the same floor plate — south-facing kitchen bathed in sun all afternoon, north-facing living end that never sees direct light. The same paint colour will look completely different in each.

This is not just about natural light. The type of artificial lighting you use — warm vs. cool LEDs, pendant height, number of points — changes how every colour reads at night. I've seen warm terracotta turn muddy and dark under cool overhead LEDs, and soft sage green look almost neon under the wrong bulb temperature.

Lighting factors to check before committing to a colour

  • Test your chosen colour at different times of day — morning, midday, and evening with your actual artificial lights on.
  • North-facing ends of an open plan benefit from warm-toned colours; avoid cool greys that can look stark.
  • South-facing areas can handle cooler tones because natural light warms them up organically.
  • Use warm-white LED bulbs (2700K–3000K) throughout open plan spaces for consistent colour rendering.
  • Pendant lights over a dining zone or island define the area and add a different quality of light intentionally.
  • Mirrors used as wall decor bounce light into darker zones and make colours look more consistent.
Pro Tip: If your open plan space has dramatically different light at each end, choose your base colour by testing it in the darkest corner. A colour that works there will look even better in the brighter zones — but not the other way around.

Achieving Colour Harmony Across Connected Living Spaces

Colour harmony in an open concept home does not mean every surface is the same colour — it means every colour in the space feels like it belongs to the same family. Think of it like a wardrobe: every item does not need to be identical, but they should all work together when laid out side by side.

The most reliable method I use with clients is the "colour story thread" — picking three to four colours that appear throughout the entire open plan, just in different proportions in different zones. One of those colours anchors every zone; the others rotate in supporting and accent roles.

Colour harmony methods that work in open layouts

Harmony Method How It Works Best For
Monochromatic One colour family in light, mid, and deep tones across zones Minimalist or Japandi styles
Analogous Neighbouring colours on the wheel — e.g. sage, olive, teal Natural, botanical, or boho styles
Complementary (muted) Opposite colours but desaturated — e.g. dusty terracotta + muted teal Eclectic or maximalist spaces
Neutral + one bold accent All base neutrals with one consistent bold colour used sparingly throughout Contemporary or Scandi spaces
Tone-on-tone Different shades of the same colour — very cohesive, very safe First-time decorators, rental properties
Pro Tip: Pull a colour palette from one piece of art or a textile you already love in the space. Nature has already done the colour harmony work for you in most good-quality prints and woven textiles — trust the source material.

How Wall Art and Decor Can Reinforce or Replace Paint Colour Zoning

Here is the thing not enough people talk about: you do not always need paint to create zones in an open concept home. Wall art, mirrors, shelving arrangements, and wall-hung decor can do almost all of the same visual work — and they are far easier to change your mind about.

A large-scale art print on one wall of a lounge zone immediately signals "this is the living area" without a single drop of paint. A gallery wall of botanical prints above a dining table tells your eye "sit down, you are in the dining zone." Decor anchors zones just as effectively as colour, and it carries personality that plain paint simply cannot.

Ways wall art and decor create zones without paint

  • A large-format art piece (canvas, framed print, or textile artwork) anchors a seating zone instantly.
  • A gallery wall arranged above a dining table signals the dining area clearly and beautifully.
  • Open wall shelving styled with colour-coordinated objects defines the zone and adds depth.
  • A macramé or textile wall hanging brings warmth and texture to a lounge zone without any commitment.
  • Mirrors used in the darker end of the open plan both brighten the space and mark it out visually.
  • A wall-mounted light fixture or sconce above a specific zone acts as a spatial signal as well as a light source.

I once styled an open plan flat for a renter who couldn't touch the walls. The landlord had painted everything the same pale cream. We used a huge woven wall textile in warm terracotta and cream above the sofa, a set of framed botanical prints above the dining table, and a round mirror in the kitchen zone. Visitors genuinely asked what colour the kitchen had been painted — they didn't realise it was all the same wall colour throughout. That is the power of well-placed decor.

Real Example: Renters and those not ready to commit to paint — this approach is made for you. Invest in three strong pieces of wall art or decor for each zone, and let them carry the colour story instead of the walls.

Colour Schemes for Open Concept Homes with Specific Style Aesthetics

Your style aesthetic shapes everything about your colour choices — not just which colours you pick, but how you layer them, how bold you go, and which materials you bring in alongside them. Colour schemes for open concept homes look very different depending on whether you are going boho, Scandi, or full maximalist.

It helps to have a clear style anchor before you start choosing colours — otherwise you end up with a space that is a bit of everything and a lot of nothing. Here is how I approach the three most popular styles I am asked about.

Style-specific colour guidance for open plan homes

  • Boho: Warm terracotta, rust, dusty pink, off-white, and ochre. Layer lots of textures — jute, linen, macramé. Zone with textile art and plants rather than paint.
  • Scandi: White or very pale greige base, one or two muted accent colours (dusty blue, sage, blush), natural wood tones throughout. Simplicity is the zone-definer.
  • Japandi: Warm white or pale clay, deep charcoal or black accents used sparingly, natural materials — linen, rattan, wood. Negative space does the zoning work.
  • Maximalist: Rich, deep jewel tones — emerald, sapphire, plum, ochre. Each zone can have its own bold colour IF they share an underlying warm or cool tone direction.
  • Contemporary/Modern: Greige or warm white base, bold accent in a single colour used consistently. Clean lines and minimal clutter let the colour scheme breathe.
  • Eclectic: Anything goes — but choose one colour that threads through every zone as a connecting stitch to keep it from feeling chaotic.

Pro Tip: If you love maximalist colour but share the space with someone who prefers calm, compromise by going maximalist in one zone (perhaps the dining area) and Scandi-neutral in the others. The contrast between zones can actually be a feature rather than a conflict.

The Role of Furniture and Textiles in Tying Colour Schemes Together

Furniture and textiles are arguably the most powerful colour carriers in an open plan space — more powerful than paint, actually, because they exist in three dimensions, they absorb and reflect light differently, and they can be changed without a decorator's invoice. A sofa, a rug, a set of dining chairs, a throw — these are your real colour tools.

The classic mistake is choosing furniture in a vacuum — picking a sofa in the shop, a dining table online, kitchen stools from somewhere else — without running them against each other first. In an open plan space where everything is visible simultaneously, this almost always results in a colour mismatch that no amount of paint can fix.

Textile and furniture colour tips for open plan spaces

  • Choose your largest furniture pieces (sofa, dining table, rug) first — they set the colour temperature of the whole space.
  • A large area rug is one of the most effective zone-definers you can buy — and it brings enormous colour into a space that paint cannot touch.
  • Cushions and throws are your cheapest colour experiment — swap them seasonally to refresh the palette.
  • Dining chairs are often underestimated as colour vehicles — a set of chairs in a bold or contrasting tone can define the dining zone beautifully.
  • Curtains or blinds carry a surprising amount of colour — make sure they are in the conversation from the start.
  • Repeat one textile colour (even in a small quantity) in each zone — a cushion here, a vase there — to create a colour thread that reads naturally from every angle.

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: Before buying any large piece of furniture, place a large sheet of paper in the colour you are considering on the floor or against the sofa. Step back and live with it for a day. It sounds daft but it has saved many of my clients from an expensive mistake.

Room-by-Room Colour Flow Examples with Visual Anchoring Tips

Let me walk you through how colour flow actually works in practice — because abstract advice about "cohesion" only gets you so far. The most useful thing I can show you is a real zone-by-zone breakdown of how colour travels through a typical open plan layout.

I'll use a common configuration: lounge zone, dining zone, and kitchen zone all sharing one floor plate, with a large window on one end and the kitchen at the other.

Zone-by-zone colour anchoring tips

  • Lounge zone: Your largest rug grounds the colour palette here. Choose it first. Wall decor above the sofa — a textile hanging, a set of art prints, or a gallery wall — defines the zone's personality.
  • Dining zone: The dining table and chairs carry the most colour. A pendant light above the table does double duty — it zones the area and adds a warm colour note. A shelf or sideboard with styled objects brings in the accent colours.
  • Kitchen zone: Cabinet colour is your biggest colour decision here. If walls are neutral, cabinets can go bolder — sage, navy, or deep grey. Repeat one colour from the lounge in ceramic accessories or small appliances.
  • Transition points: Identify where one zone ends and another begins. Put something there — a plant, a floor lamp, an open shelving unit — to act as a visual "comma" in the space.
  • The connecting thread: Choose one colour that appears somewhere in every zone, even in a small way. This creates subconscious cohesion that reads as "this home is put together" even to guests who couldn't tell you why.

I worked on a long, narrow Victorian terrace conversion where the open plan stretched about twelve metres from front to back. The challenge was keeping it from feeling like a corridor. We anchored each zone with a different rug — same colour family, different scale of pattern — and used a single brass tone in hardware, light fittings, and a few accessories across all three zones. That brass thread made the whole space sing. Nobody asked why it felt cohesive; they just sat down and relaxed. That is exactly what you want.

Real Example: The "connector colour" trick — picking one metallic, one neutral tone, or one shade of green that appears in every single zone, even if just in a small ceramic or a trailing plant — is the single easiest way to make an open plan space feel intentionally designed rather than randomly assembled.

Budget-Friendly Ways to Test and Commit to an Open Concept Colour Palette

Committing to a colour palette across an entire open plan space is genuinely daunting — not just emotionally but financially. Getting it wrong in a big space means a lot of wasted paint, or worse, furniture you need to sell on. The good news is there are very practical ways to test before you commit, and most of them cost very little.

I always tell clients: think of the first round as "renting the colour." You are not marrying it yet. You are just seeing how you get on.

Low-cost ways to test an open plan colour palette

  • Order paint tester pots and apply them to A2 or A3 card, not directly on the wall — you can move them around and test them across all zones.
  • Use cushion covers and throws in your intended accent colours before committing to a sofa or curtains — cushions are your cheapest experiment.
  • Buy one affordable print in your intended accent colour palette and live with it for two weeks before buying more wall art or repainting.
  • Try peel-and-stick paint samples if your wall is already white — some brands offer these and they remove cleanly.
  • Use large pieces of coloured card or even wrapping paper to mock up what a coloured accent wall will look like before painting it.
  • Rearrange and style the furniture you already have in zone formations before spending anything — this often reveals what is actually missing.
  • Visit a local paint store that offers physical colour consultations — many offer this free of charge and it is worth every minute.

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: The most budget-friendly route into a new colour palette is always through textiles and art first, paint second. Swap your cushions and throws, buy one or two art prints, and live with the new palette for a month before touching the walls. You will be absolutely certain by then — or happily grateful you did not reach for the paintbrush.

Open Concept Living Room Colour Looks: Visual Inspiration for Every Style

Here is a curated look at how different colour schemes actually come to life across open concept spaces — from understated Scandi schemes to full maximalist colour celebrations.

  • Cosy Minimalism Home Decor Trend - Unified tones across flowing spaces
  • Transitional Interior Design Trend - Balanced colour flow between rooms

More About Getting Colour Right in Open Plan Homes

Getting colour right in an open concept home is one of the most rewarding decorating challenges you will take on — and the learning curve is genuinely worth it.

The key things to hold onto are: start with a versatile base, use accent colours purposefully to zone and add personality, and remember that paint is only one part of the picture. Wall art, textiles, rugs, lighting, and carefully chosen decor objects all carry colour just as powerfully. For a thorough practical guide on how to actually approach the painting process in an open concept layout — including advice on where to stop and start each colour — I'd recommend reading this guide by How to Paint an Open-Concept Home | Sherwin-Williams, which covers the technical side really well.

The most important thing? Do not let the scale of an open plan space paralyse you into beige inaction. Start small, test often, and build your confidence one zone at a time.

Ready to Start Your Open Concept Colour Story?

I hope this has given you a real, practical framework to approach colour schemes in your open concept home — not just a list of pretty colours, but an actual method for making the space feel considered and cohesive from every angle.

Whether you are starting from scratch, repainting, or simply looking to refresh the feel of your open plan through art and decor rather than a full renovation, the principles here apply. Take it one zone at a time, trust your base colour, and let the textiles and art do far more of the heavy lifting than most people realise.

I'd genuinely love to know — what is the trickiest part of your open plan space to get right? Is it a dark corner, a tricky zone transition, or just too much beige that came with the house? Drop it in the comments — let's figure it out together.

Choosing a colour palette for wall art is one of the most satisfying — and most confusing — parts of decorating a room. The good news is that it doesn't have to be guesswork. With a few simple principles and a clear starting point, you can build a palette that feels intentional, cohesive, and genuinely "you".

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in a room you love the furniture in, bought a piece of wall art that seemed perfect in the shop, hung it up at home — and felt that nagging sense that something was just... off? You're not alone. It happens to almost everyone, and it's almost never about taste. It's about colour.

Quick answer: Start with the colours already in your room — your sofa, rug, curtains — and pick wall art that either echoes one of those tones or adds a considered contrast. Aim for a palette of two to four colours maximum, and use the 60-30-10 rule to keep things balanced. Once you have your anchor colour, everything else follows.

A colour palette for a room is simply the set of colours that appear across your walls, furniture, textiles, and accessories — and your wall art sits within that system, not apart from it. When art is chosen to work with that palette, the whole room lifts. When it's chosen in isolation, it can feel like an afterthought. If you're looking to make a real statement, browsing unique wall art with colour in mind will make the selection process so much easier — and if you want to extend the look beyond your walls, exploring unique home decor items in complementary tones ties the whole room together beautifully.

How to Choose a Colour Palette for Wall Art

The very first step is to stop looking at the art and start looking at your room. Your existing colours are your brief. Everything else — the art, the accessories, the finishing touches — needs to respond to what's already there.

Begin by identifying the three dominant colours in your space: the main wall colour, your largest piece of furniture, and your floor or rug. These three form your foundation. Your wall art should share at least one of these tones, or introduce a new colour that sits harmoniously alongside them.

A bright, airy living room with warm white walls, a dusty sage green linen sofa, a jute rug in natural oat tones, and a wooden coffee table. Paint swatches and fabric samples are laid out on the sofa in coordinating muted tones — sage, terracotta, and warm cream. A South Asian woman in her early thirties sits on the sofa, relaxed, cross-legged, studying the swatches thoughtfully in natural morning light.]]

Step-by-step: Building your wall art colour palette

  • Collect your room's colours. Grab a cushion, a paint chip from the wall, or a photo of your rug and use it as your reference point.
  • Choose an anchor colour. This is the one colour your art must include. It's usually your most dominant room tone.
  • Add one supporting colour. This can be a lighter or darker variation of the anchor, or a harmonious neighbour on the colour wheel.
  • Allow one accent. A small pop of contrast — a terracotta against a sage, or a blush against a navy — is what gives the room life.
  • Stick to a maximum of four colours across all your art. More than that and the wall starts to feel chaotic.

I worked with a client once who had a beautiful deep teal sofa and kept buying art with bright, saturated colours because she loved colour in general. The room never felt right. When we pulled back and found a soft burnt orange — the exact warm undertone already hiding in her wooden floorboards — and sourced art in teal, burnt orange, and cream, the room transformed. Same sofa. Same floor. Different art. Completely different room.

Pro Tip: Take a photo of your room on your phone and use the colour picker in any free editing app to extract the exact hex codes of your dominant colours. Then search for art using those tones as your filter. It takes five minutes and saves a lot of returning and re-ordering.

How to Match Wall Art Colours to Your Existing Room Decor

Matching doesn't mean matchy-matchy. You're not trying to find art that's the same colour as your cushions — you're looking for art that belongs in the same family. Think of it like putting together an outfit: the pieces don't have to match exactly, but they need to work together.

The most reliable method is what I call the "pull and echo" approach. You pull one colour from an existing element in the room — a textured rug, a velvet cushion, a plant pot — and you echo it in the art. Even a small area of that colour in the artwork is enough to create a visual thread.

Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. A cosy, eclectic living room with a dusty blue feature wall, a boucle cream armchair, a rust-toned throw, and a potted fiddle leaf fig in a terracotta planter. A collection of decorative objects in coordinating warm tones is arranged on a low wooden sideboard. A Black woman in her mid-forties with natural hair stands beside the sideboard, holding a terracotta plant pot up next to the blue wall, comparing the tones with a warm, thoughtful expression.]]

What to look for when matching art to your room

  • Soft furnishings first. Your sofa and rug carry the most colour surface area — let them lead.
  • Check your undertones. A "grey" room might have cool blue undertones or warm pink ones. Your art should share the same undertone family.
  • Don't ignore neutrals. Cream, oat, putty, and stone all have warmth or coolness built in. Art with similar neutral tones will always feel at home.
  • Consider the floor. Wooden floors add warmth; stone or concrete adds cool. Let that inform whether your art leans warm or cool.
  • Use your plants. The green of foliage is one of the most reliable bridge colours — it works with almost any palette and adds life.
Real Example: A client with an all-white room felt it was "too cold." Rather than repainting, we chose art with warm ochre, dusty blush, and raw linen tones. Within a week, people were commenting that the room felt "warmer" — without a single piece of furniture having changed.

Popular Colour Palette Styles and Combinations for Wall Art

Some colour combinations are popular for a reason — they work reliably across a huge range of interior styles and room sizes. Knowing the go-to pairings saves a lot of time when you're browsing art and gives you a confident starting point.

The mistake I always see is people going straight to a colour they love without checking if it fits any recognisable palette. Even if your instinct is good, having a named palette gives you a framework — and a framework means you can shop with purpose.

Tried-and-tested colour palette combinations for wall art

  • Warm neutrals: Cream, oat, sand, and terracotta. Works in almost any home and age beautifully. Perfect for a living room or hallway.
  • Cool coastal: White, soft navy, sky blue, and seafoam. Crisp and fresh, great for bathrooms and bedrooms near the sea or with light-filled windows.
  • Earthy botanical: Olive, sage, rust, and warm brown. Works brilliantly with natural materials — rattan, linen, and wood.
  • Moody jewel tones: Deep teal, mustard, burgundy, and charcoal. Dramatic and luxurious — ideal for a dining room or a home office with personality.
  • Scandi minimal: White, pale grey, black, and a single soft accent like blush or pale green. Clean, calm, and endlessly versatile.

How Colour Theory Applies to Choosing Wall Art

You don't need to be an artist to use colour theory — you just need to know the three most useful concepts: complementary colours, analogous colours, and the 60-30-10 rule. These three ideas will answer most of your colour questions about wall art.

Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the colour wheel — blue and orange, green and red, purple and yellow. Using them in art creates energy and contrast. Analogous colours sit next to each other — blue-green, green, and yellow-green. These feel calm and cohesive, great for a bedroom or meditation space.

[[IMG|colour-theory-wall-art-selection|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. Below, three clearly labelled visual sections side by side: Left section labelled "Complementary" shows a simple colour wheel with two opposing colours highlighted (blue and orange). Centre section labelled "Analogous" shows three adjacent colour wheel segments highlighted (blue-green, green, yellow-green). Right section labelled "60-30-10 Rule" shows a simple room floor-plan icon divided proportionally into three shaded zones labelled 60% dominant, 30% secondary, 10% accent. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Colour theory rules to apply when choosing wall art

  • 60-30-10 rule: 60% of your room should be the dominant colour (walls, large furniture), 30% secondary (soft furnishings, curtains), and 10% accent — your wall art can carry the 10% accent colour without overwhelming the room.
  • Complementary contrast: If your room is mostly cool blue, an art piece with warm amber or terracotta will make both colours sing.
  • Analogous harmony: If you want a calm, restful room, choose art in tones close to your existing wall colour — slightly lighter or darker, or a nearby shade.
  • Temperature check: Warm colours (reds, yellows, oranges) advance — they feel closer and more energising. Cool colours (blues, greens, purples) recede — they feel further away and more calming.
  • Saturation balance: If your room is low saturation (muted tones), introducing highly saturated art can jar. Aim to match the saturation level of art to the room's existing intensity.
Pro Tip: A quick way to check if your art's colours are analogous or complementary to your room is to use a free colour wheel app on your phone. Simply enter the hex code of your wall colour and it'll show you the complementary and analogous options instantly. No design degree required.

Room-by-Room Colour Palette Recommendations for Wall Art

Different rooms have different jobs. A bedroom needs to rest you; a kitchen needs to energise you; a hallway needs to welcome you. The colour palette of your wall art should support whatever that room is asking of the people in it.

I find this is the area where most online guides completely let people down — they give generic colour theory without saying "in your bathroom, try this; in your child's room, try that." So here's the practical version, room by room.

How to Use a Colour Palette Generator or Tool to Pick Wall Art

If you find colour matching difficult to do by eye, a colour palette generator is genuinely one of the most useful tools available — and the best ones are free. You simply upload a photo of your room and the tool extracts the dominant colours for you, showing you the exact tones you're working with.

Once you have those colours, you can use them to filter your art search by tone, or simply use them as a reference when browsing. It makes the whole process far more objective and takes a lot of the anxiety out of choosing.

She looks engaged and focused, caught in a natural candid moment.]]

How to get the most from a colour palette tool

  • Use a photo taken in daylight. Artificial lighting changes colours dramatically. A photo taken on a cloudy day gives the most accurate reading of your room's real tones.
  • Try Coolors, Adobe Color, or Canva's colour extractor. All three allow you to upload a photo and extract a palette from it — no account needed for most features.
  • Look for the undertones, not just the main colours. The tool will often reveal a warm or cool bias you hadn't consciously noticed.
  • Save your palette as a screenshot. Use it to shop from. Having it on your phone means you can compare art to it instantly, even in physical shops.
  • Generate a complementary palette too. Most tools have a "complementary" or "contrast" option — this is great for finding an accent colour to introduce through your art.
Pro Tip: If you're torn between two art options, photograph each one on your phone screen (or in your tab) next to your saved room palette screenshot. Your eye will tell you immediately which one belongs in the room and which one fights it.

Mixing and Matching Multiple Pieces of Wall Art Using a Cohesive Palette

Gallery walls are one of my favourite things to style — but they're also one of the easiest to get wrong. The most common mistake I see is people choosing pieces they love individually without checking that they belong to the same colour family. The result is a wall that looks busy rather than curated.

The fix is simple: decide on your shared palette before you start buying. Every piece in your gallery wall should include at least one of your chosen palette colours. It doesn't have to be the dominant colour — even a small area of it is enough to create the visual thread that ties the collection together.

[[IMG|mixing-matching-multiple-wall-art-pieces-gallery|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — macramé hangings, wall shelves with ceramic objects, wall-mounted sconces — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A warm, lived-in dining room with a terracotta-toned feature wall, a round oak dining table with mismatched chairs in warm tones, a woven pendant light, and a wooden shelf displaying ceramic bowls and small sculptural objects in earthy tones. A mixed-heritage couple — a woman in her late thirties and a man in his early forties — are rearranging decorative objects on the shelf together, laughing, in warm late-afternoon light.]]

Tips for building a cohesive multi-piece wall art collection

  • Set a palette cap of three to four colours. Every piece in the collection must include at least one of them, no exceptions.
  • Vary the tone, not the colour. Using light sage, mid sage, and deep sage across different pieces creates depth without discord.
  • Use a unifying frame colour. If the art itself varies, matching all your frames in one colour (black, natural oak, or white) creates visual order instantly.
  • Mix abstract and representational pieces. An abstract in earthy tones alongside a botanical print in the same tones creates a collected, curated feel.
  • Leave breathing room. At least a hand-width of space between pieces helps each one read clearly rather than competing.
  • Mock it up before you hang. Lay everything on the floor first. Photograph it from above. Review the colour balance from the photo — it's much more revealing than looking at it in person on the floor.
[[PRODUCT|gallery wall art set in earthy tones for living rooms]]
Real Example: I once helped a client who had bought eight individual prints she adored, but the wall looked chaotic. When we compared them all side by side, we discovered five of them had warm terracotta as an undertone and three were purely cool. We moved the cool ones to her home office and replaced them with terracotta-toned pieces. The gallery wall went from noisy to genuinely beautiful — and all we did was edit the palette.

Seasonal and Trend-Led Colour Palettes for Wall Art in 2024–2025

Trends matter less in interiors than they do in fashion, but they're still worth knowing — especially if you want your space to feel current without being a slave to the moment. The best approach is to use trend colours as your accent, not your foundation.

In 2024–2025, the mood in home interiors has moved decisively toward warmth, earthiness, and a kind of quiet richness. Gone is the cool grey dominance of the previous decade — the palette of the moment is warmer, more grounded, and honestly more liveable.

[[IMG|seasonal-trend-colour-palettes-wall-art-2024-2025|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, warm earthy Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — wall-mounted shelves with dried botanical stems, a woven macramé wall hanging, ceramic wall-mounted planters — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A rich, textured living space with warm terracotta walls, a low boucle sofa in warm oat, a deep sage velvet cushion, a chunky jute rug, and dried pampas grass in a tall ceramic vase. A South-East Asian woman in her late thirties sits cross-legged on the rug with a mug of tea, looking relaxed and contemplative in golden late-afternoon light.]]

Key colour trends for wall art in 2024–2025

  • Warm terracotta and clay. The undisputed colour of the moment. Works beautifully in living rooms and dining spaces, especially alongside natural materials.
  • Sage and olive green. Perennially popular, but 2024 sees them shift slightly darker — more forest, less mint. Gorgeous in bathrooms and bedrooms.
  • Warm chocolate brown. Rich, grounding, and surprisingly versatile. Art in warm brown tones works brilliantly in home offices and studies.
  • Dusty blush and warm rose. Not the millennial pink of a decade ago — this is more muted, more sophisticated, and pairs wonderfully with warm wood tones.
  • Deep burgundy and wine. A more daring choice, but one that's growing fast. Think rich textural art in velvet-like tones for dining rooms and snugs.
  • Natural off-white and raw linen. Not white-white, but warm, raw, organic tones — oat, ecru, unbleached linen. These act as the neutral base that makes all the above sing.
Pro Tip: Rather than redecorating seasonally, buy one or two smaller art pieces or prints in a trend colour and rotate them in. Your foundation decor stays constant — the accent art is what shifts the feeling with the season.

How Wall Art Finish (Matte, Canvas, Print) Affects Colour Perception

This is the one thing almost no one talks about when choosing wall art — and it can completely change how a colour looks once it's in your home. The same artwork reproduced on a glossy print, a matte print, and a canvas will look noticeably different in real life, even if the underlying colours are identical.

Understanding how finish affects colour means you can make better choices when shopping online, where you can't hold the piece up to the light yourself. Here's what you need to know.

Inspiring Wall Art Colour Palette Styles and Looks

Sometimes the best way to find your palette is to see it in action across a range of real styles and aesthetic directions. Whether you're drawn to the calm of Japandi, the warmth of Mediterranean, or the graphic confidence of mid-century modern, your colour palette for wall art follows naturally from the look you love.

  • Modern Contemporary Home Decor Trend - Bold curated colour for modern art
  • Eclectic Maximalist Home Decor Trend - Rich layered hues inspiring wall art

What Else You Should Know About Colour and Wall Art

One thing that often surprises people is that the wall colour and the art don't need to match — in fact, choosing your art first and working backward to find the right wall colour is a completely valid (and often more satisfying) approach.

It's a method championed by galleries and interior designers alike, and it's explored really well in this piece from Saatchi Art: How to Choose the Perfect Wall Color to Complement Your Art | Canvas: A Blog By Saatchi Art. The idea is that great art has inherent colour relationships built into it, and a supportive wall colour simply lets those relationships breathe.

When you approach it this way, the art becomes the starting point — and the room is built around it. For most of us, that's the opposite of how we've been told to decorate. But it works brilliantly, particularly if you're starting with a blank canvas (no pun intended) or redecorating a room from scratch.

It also takes the pressure off finding "the right" art for a room you've already committed to. Instead, you find art you love, extract its palette, and let that guide your paint, your textiles, and your accessories. It's more flexible — and far more personal.

Putting It All Together — Your Colour Palette, Your Walls, Your Home

Choosing a colour palette for wall art doesn't have to be stressful or complicated. Start with what you already have, identify the colours that are already doing the work in your room, and look for art that joins that conversation rather than starting a new one.

Use the tools available to you — a colour picker app, a palette generator, a simple photograph. Trust your instincts when two colours feel like they belong together, and trust the process when they don't. Colour is one of the most powerful things in a home, and your wall art is one of the few parts of a room you can swap out relatively easily as your taste evolves.

The most important thing I always say to clients is this: choose art you genuinely love, in colours that feel right for where you are right now. A beautiful piece of art in a colour that moves you will always find its place in a home — even if it takes a little rearranging to get there.

So — what's the one room in your home where the colour feels most "off" to you right now, and what do you think is missing from the palette?

how do i hang heavy framed art safely?.bodyHtml:
If you want to hang heavy framed art safely, the short answer is this: you need the right hardware for your specific wall type, you must know the exact weight of your piece, and you should never trust a single small nail for anything over 5 lbs. Get those three things right and your artwork stays on the wall — and off the floor.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in front of a beautiful, oversized framed piece and felt that little knot of anxiety — the one that whispers, "what if it falls in the night?" I've been there, and so have most of my clients. The good news is that wall art of any size can go up safely when you follow the right process from the start.

Quick answer: To hang heavy framed art safely, identify your wall type (drywall, plaster or brick), choose hardware rated well above your frame's actual weight, and always anchor into a stud or use a wall anchor rated for the load. A French cleat or two heavy-duty D-rings are almost always a better choice than picture wire alone for anything over 20 lbs.

Hanging a large, heavy frame is one of those home tasks that looks simple but has a surprising number of ways to go wrong. Whether you're dealing with unique wall art that's a real centrepiece investment or adding a collection of statement pieces to your unique home decor, understanding the basics of safe installation means your walls — and your artwork — stay in perfect condition for years.

What Actually Counts as "Heavy" Framed Art? Specific Weight Thresholds Explained

Most people assume "heavy" means something enormous, but in the world of picture hanging, weight thresholds matter a lot sooner than you might think. Understanding exactly where the boundaries sit will save you from guessing — and from a frame on the floor at 2am.

[[IMG|weight-thresholds-heavy-framed-art|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Weight Thresholds for Framed Art", then a clear VISUAL comparison with three labelled sections side by side: left section labelled "Light: Under 5 lbs — single small nail or adhesive strip", centre section labelled "Medium: 5–20 lbs — two nails into studs or wall anchors", right section labelled "Heavy: Over 20 lbs — French cleat, heavy-duty D-rings, or stud-mounted hardware". Use simple icon-style scales or weight symbols above each label. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

The Weight Brackets You Need to Know

  • Under 5 lbs: A small print in a lightweight frame. A single picture hook or an adhesive strip rated for the weight is usually fine.
  • 5–20 lbs: Medium weight — think a canvas print in a standard timber frame. Two hooks or a wall anchor rated to at least double the actual weight is the right move here.
  • 20–50 lbs: This is where "heavy" begins. You need stud fixings, heavy-duty anchors, or a French cleat. Don't rely on picture wire alone at this weight.
  • Over 50 lbs: Anything above this is genuinely heavy. Think large oil paintings in ornate gilded frames, oversized mirrors framed in solid wood, or multi-panel art installations. Professional-grade hardware and often a second pair of hands — or a professional installer — are strongly advised.
  • Over 100 lbs: At this point, professional installation should be your default unless you have significant DIY experience and the right tools.

I once had a client who swore her framed botanical print was "basically nothing" — turned out it was a solid hardwood frame with UV glass and it weighed just over 30 lbs. She'd hung it on two small nails in plasterboard with no anchors. We rehung it properly on a French cleat screwed into two studs and she said it felt like a completely different experience — solid, confident, safe.

Pro Tip: Before you buy any hardware, weigh your frame. Pop it on your bathroom scales — hold it, note the reading, then put it down and subtract your own weight. It takes 30 seconds and tells you exactly which bracket you're in.
